So exceedingly was he made.”
Thus the warrior Seytek reflected,
His father appearing before his eyes,
His mind bewildered and divided,
And now he stood content.
His first forefather was Tügöl Khan;
Kara Khan never leaves his descendants.
The sharp steel sword truly has a sheath.
The people clamored and raised a tumult,
The nation went about in uproar—
It was no lie but the truth.
May God never take away a father;
May no child be left behind
Without knowing his father alive.
If the Creator is indeed true,
May He never inflict such humiliation
Upon one of His servants.
My heart was troubled with grief;
This time my eyes have seen
My gray-maned lion father,
So I bear no grievance against God.
He is both bloodthirsty and lionhearted;
All twelve limbs of my dear
Gray-maned father are whole.
See how he burns and cries out.
Father and son have met;
See how they surge with emotion.
To embrace each other once,
Making heaven and earth resound,
To greet each other just once—
See how they burn with longing.
The hero Semetey
Had no words to speak,
No eyes with which to gaze,
No potent medicine to restore him;
Such filth is this world.
The generous lion, led astray,
Met his own son,
Yet stood there without recognizing him.
Semetey then spoke these words,
Telling of horrors before their meeting:
“Born of a mother, I became a lion;
I brought the whole world beneath my rule,
And became a gray-maned lion of a man.
Led astray by the enemy,
I became one who fled his people.
I took a cavern for my home;
I turned back after my people were scattered,
And was separated from Külchoro,
Who had sat there as my protector.
I scouted the land and grieved;
I was parted from mother, child, and wife,
From my Kyrgyz people with their cities,
And from all those who remained.
A person longs for one to ride;
She lured me and bound me.
Kökmonchok, daughter of the peri,
Aichürök’s younger sister,
Grew up and blocked my road,
Bewitched me and bound my hands,
And showed me many wonders.
I am not dead but alive,
One of those who have not died.
She bound my eyes so I could not see,
And chewed me between her teeth.
Those she stabbed were countless and turned to ash;
Her army numbered tens of thousands.
The steel city was a great fortress;
By my reckoning, my father was mighty.
Defeated by the Jediger,
Why was my noble father, that dear lion,
Reduced to such humiliation?
He filled and dammed the broad yellow valley,
Growing stronger each time he died,
Smoldering anew whenever he was spent,
And gaining strength from his very roots.
Each time he died, he flourished;
He was both sovereign and lionhearted.
My oceanic, gray-maned lion father
Was blessed with perfect fortune;
Indeed, my father was so great a hero.
That I was made Semetey’s son
Leaves me no grievance against God.
I heard tales among the people,
But now I have seen my father’s word made flesh.
Left an orphan, I grew to manhood,
Managed to rejoin my homeland,
Matured and became a warrior,
And became the equal of heroic sons;
Now I have seen my father himself.
More than his teeming host,
I have seen my father’s own eyes.
My soul is aflame, my breast an ember,
Yet my heart is content with the Creator.
I longed to see my father,
And now not the slightest regret remains.
My heart is content with the Maker;
I have seen the mountain that is my support,
I have seen my valiant father.
My towering presence, like the Ala-Too—
My heart surges, my insides boil,
And I am filled with true joy:
I have seen my father’s form.”
So saying, his son,
The sovereign among women.
A bright sun fashioned by God,
A paradise among women, a sacred night—
My dear mother Kanykey,
Can she be a living soul who has not died?
My dear mother, this paradise,
Can she still be alive, not dead?
If only my mother would come quickly;
Facing toward the qibla,
With sharp steel for my pillow,
Let me open my mouth as wide as a cavern.
Let her bare her right breast,
Let her feed this ash-starved one,
Press my wretched self to her bosom,
And nurse me like a little child.
If my cavernous mouth opens,
If my poor mother is still alive,
And white breast milk is sprinkled in my mouth,
I shall be freed from this affliction.
My lion-born, heroic younger brother,
My brave brother guarded by the spirit,
Then I shall turn to you.
I shall look into your eyes.”
As he spoke thus,
Old Mother Kanykey wept,
Saying, “The bloodthirsty hero has come to this,”
And all the people watching wept.
No tiny soul could leave without crying out;
The sorrowful sobbed and wept.
His wretched mother Kanykey
Would have died without regret;
Not a fly-sized shred of life remained in her.
Her heart heaved and her body melted,
She swayed like a graceful gray pacer,
Rocked like molten lead,
Her body loosening and trembling;
All twelve sinews and eighty bones
Melted without remainder and trembled.
Her whole body shuddered,
And white milk tingled in her breasts.
“The sorcerers joined together
And carried me away.
I was led astray and passed on,
Parted from my people and gone.
In Jelpiniş beneath the earth,
I remained here for three years.
Of the pleasures of this world
I have often had my fill.
In the desert of Medina,
On the shore of Jan Baspas,
I remained there for three years.
Then I turned and came back;
I know that I arrived
At this black cave of the local sorcerer.
Eighty maidens are my soul-companions,
And I live in their company.
Once I ruled a people and maintained a nation,
But my greatness too was left behind;
Unable to hear or see,
I suffer here in misery.
Is my bloodthirsty head truly that of a khan?
To attain my heart’s desire,
To turn and return to my people,
To the city with its palace and the troubled nation,
To go back there again,
To find once more my brother, child, and wife—
To find and reclaim them,
My timely words have come too late,
And my two eyes have strained into four.
Hearing Külchoro’s voice clearly,
My old affliction stirred anew.
When I heard this, Külchoro,
Enemy of the infidel,
I halted and mourned an ancient grief.
If you truly are Külchoro,
And I am truly your gray-maned lion,
Then are my spoken words mere lament?
The finest wearer of a flowing dress,
The most gracious among women,
The purest of the long-haired,
My noble mother, my valiant one.
My need while this life is held in trust,
My radiant-browed angel.
My precious mother,
Who sat as my protector.
Bare your breast, and let me kiss it;
If you offer your breast, let me suckle.
If pure white milk flows from it,
The illness rooted in my bones will depart,
All sorrow will vanish,
And your son will recover once more.
If milk flows from your breast,
Then God has truly granted our desire.
If black blood flows from your breast,
Then God has truly struck us down.
If pure white milk flows from your breast,
Then God has brightened His countenance;
Your lion will return again,
All anguish will scatter,
And his eyes will open wide.
Your grief and sorrow will vanish,
And your fortunes will mend again.
If dark-black blood flows,
Bow your head before grief
And cut off all your hope.
Let your Venus-like eyes shine.
Kanykey and old Bakai,
Tear wounds in your own flesh.
Behold the true world;
You elders who truly grieve,
Die without further torment.
My white wife Aichürök,
Loosen your hair until it darkens the earth,
Claw your bloodied face,
Put on black and sob,
Crying, ‘My dear prince has died,’
Put on black and wail.
Companion of this present age,
O Külchoro, brother of my nest,
Speak words that could shatter mountains.”
He had lain there peacefully.
Before anyone could say another word,
His poor mother sobbed,
Every tiny bone in her body shuddered,
Her body went limp and tossed about.
Pleading, “My Morning Star,”
She bared her breast and settled down,
Crooning, “My flower-like colt.”
When his mother came near,
His troubled heart found peace.
The poor lion guarded by the spirit said,
“My mother’s scent has come;
The Creator has granted me goodness.
If only I see her, my heart will be content;
I have no sanctuary but my mother.
One day I shall meet death and die;
Before the five stars of the wild sheep set,
What can I do
For my valiant mother, my sanctuary?
When I was an infant,
I clung to you, wailing and crying.
When six months had passed,
I fought for your breast.
In the seventh month you swelled with me;
When eight months had passed,
I kicked your dress until it tore.
You made my valor surpass all others;
I chafed the flesh of your calves,
Made your heels ache,
And blood flow from your legs.
You invoked God, moaning in anguish,
